mcq.prompt: What exactly is a translation unit?
choices: One source file as written on disk
One source file after preprocessing, with every #include pasted in and every macro expanded
All source files of one library, seen together
One object file after assembly
mcq.explain: A translation unit is the post-preprocessing text: the .cpp plus the contents of everything it included, with macros expanded. That is the only thing the compiler ever sees at once — it never sees 'the project'. Confusing the file on disk with the translation unit is what makes header changes feel like they should be free.

mcq.prompt: Which stage reports `undefined reference to spread_bps(Order const&)`?
choices: Preprocessing
Compilation
Assembly
Linking
mcq.explain: The compiler is satisfied once a declaration gives it the name and type; whether a definition exists anywhere in the program is a question only the linker, holding every selected object file, can answer. That is the chapter's rule in practice: a compile error belongs to one translation unit, a linker error is a disagreement among translation units or libraries.

mcq.prompt: `pricing.hpp` is edited. `main.cpp` is not. Why must main.o be rebuilt anyway?
choices: Because main.cpp's translation unit contains the pasted header text, so its input has changed
Because the linker compares timestamps and refuses stale objects
Because the header's include guard macro changes on every edit
It need not be; separate compilation exists precisely to avoid that
mcq.explain: Separate compilation saves work in the other direction — editing main.cpp does not force pricing.cpp to be recompiled. But every translation unit that included the header contains a pasted copy of it, so a header edit changes their input text. Reusing a stale object can preserve an old class layout or an old declaration, and the linker will not notice: it matches symbol names, not source-level intent.

mcq.prompt: How far does an include guard's protection reach?
choices: Until the guard macro is #undef'd anywhere in the program
The whole program, so a header is pasted at most once per build
One preprocessing run, so each translation unit still gets its own copy
One directory of source files
mcq.explain: Guard state is macro state, and macro state lasts only for the current preprocessing run. Both pricing.cpp and main.cpp independently paste one guarded copy of pricing.hpp, so the class definition and the inline function definitions really do appear in both translation units. What makes that legal is the ODR's allowance for classes, inline entities and templates — not the guard.

mcq.prompt: `#define SQUARE(x) x * x` and `SQUARE(a + b)` with a = 2, b = 3. What is the result?
choices: 25, as a function would give
11, because the expansion is a + b * a + b
A compile error from the missing parentheses
Unspecified, because the order of evaluation is not fixed
mcq.explain: The preprocessor substitutes tokens before the compiler knows anything about types or precedence, so the call expands to a + b * a + b — that is 2 + 3*2 + 3, or 11. Parenthesising the parameters and the whole expansion fixes this particular defect, but it does not fix repeated evaluation of an argument with side effects. A constexpr function has neither problem.

mcq.prompt: A non-inline free function is defined in a header included by three .cpp files. What happens?
choices: The linker reports multiple definition, because each translation unit emits a definition
The compiler rejects the second inclusion
The linker silently keeps one, as it does for inline functions
Nothing; the include guard prevents duplicates
mcq.explain: Each of the three translation units emits a strong definition of the same linker-visible name, and the ODR permits only one for a non-inline function, so the linker cannot choose. Marking it inline is what changes the emitted symbol into a weak/COMDAT definition the linker is allowed to deduplicate; the include guard only stops a second copy inside one translation unit.

mcq.prompt: Which of these at namespace scope is a declaration but NOT a definition?
choices: extern int tick_count = 0;
inline int tick_count = 0;
int tick_count;
extern int tick_count;
mcq.explain: extern with no initialiser only announces that a definition with external linkage exists elsewhere. Plain `int tick_count;` at namespace scope both declares and defines. Adding an initialiser makes even the extern form a definition, and an inline variable is a definition that may legally appear in every translation unit that includes it.

mcq.prompt: What does the `inline` keyword primarily mean in modern C++?
choices: That the function is emitted into every caller's object file and never called indirectly
That the optimiser must substitute the function body at each call site
That identical definitions may appear in several translation units and denote one entity
That the function has internal linkage
mcq.explain: inline is an ODR permission, not an optimisation directive: it says the same definition may legally appear in many translation units. The optimiser inlines functions that lack the keyword and declines to inline functions that carry it. An inline function keeps external linkage — that is exactly what lets all those definitions denote one entity, which is the opposite of internal linkage.

mcq.prompt: Two .cpp files each define a `struct Helper` with different members plus an out-of-class `inline void Helper::normalize()`. They are compiled and linked together. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: It links cleanly, one weak definition is retained, and the program has undefined behaviour
It links cleanly and each file uses its own version, which is well-defined
The compiler rejects one of the files
The linker reports multiple definition of Helper::normalize
mcq.explain: Both inline member definitions become weak or COMDAT symbols with the same mangled name, so the linker retains one and discards the other without comparing bodies. Whichever survives is used by both callers — one of which believes in a different layout. No diagnostic is required, and the symptom can change with optimisation level or link order. Weak binding is what makes the ODR violation silent; it is not what makes it legal.

mcq.prompt: An inline function is defined in two headers as `return rate * 2;` and `return 2 * rate;`. Both are included in different translation units. What is the verdict?
choices: Fine, because multiplication is commutative and the results agree
An ODR violation, because the token sequences differ
Fine, because inline functions are exempt from the ODR
A compile error in whichever translation unit is compiled second
mcq.explain: The ODR's allowance for multiple inline definitions requires them to be the same definition — matching token sequences, with names looking up to the same entities. 'Produces equal results' is not the test. The two translation units are compiled independently, so nothing compares them; the program is simply ill-formed with no diagnostic required.

mcq.prompt: A function-local `static unsigned long call_count = 0;` — what are its storage duration, scope and linkage?
choices: Static duration, namespace scope, internal linkage
Thread duration, block scope, no linkage
Static duration, block scope, no linkage
Automatic duration, block scope, internal linkage
mcq.explain: The object lives for the whole program, its name is visible only inside the enclosing block, and no declaration elsewhere can denote it — three independent answers to three independent questions. Reading 'static' as one concept is the trap: at block scope the keyword grants storage duration, at namespace scope it grants internal linkage, and inside a class it declares a member shared by all instances.

mcq.prompt: What does the keyword `static` do at namespace scope?
choices: Makes the variable const
Makes the definition inline
Gives the entity static storage duration, which it would not otherwise have
Gives the name internal linkage
mcq.explain: A namespace-scope object already has static storage duration; what the keyword adds there is internal linkage, so no other translation unit can denote the same entity. Granting storage duration is what the same keyword does at block scope. Ask which property the context changes rather than treating the word as one concept.

mcq.prompt: A function is defined inside an anonymous namespace. What is true of it?
choices: It has no linkage, like a block-scope name
It has internal linkage, and it has no storage duration because it is not an object
It has internal linkage and automatic storage duration
It has external linkage but hidden visibility
mcq.explain: An anonymous-namespace name has internal linkage, so another translation unit may spell the same function without denoting it. Storage duration classifies objects and references, not functions, so the question simply does not apply. Visibility is a third, separate thing — a shared library's export table — and is not what an anonymous namespace controls.

mcq.prompt: Why does the chapter prefer an anonymous namespace over namespace-scope `static` for translation-unit-local helpers?
choices: An anonymous namespace also localises types, which static cannot do
static gives external linkage to types
An anonymous namespace has no runtime cost, unlike static
static is deprecated in C++23
mcq.explain: Namespace-scope static gives internal linkage to functions and variables only; there is no way to apply it to a class. An anonymous namespace covers types as well, which is exactly what the two-file Helper collision needed. Both spellings remain legal — static survives mainly as C-compatible style — and neither has a runtime cost.

mcq.prompt: Why can two `extern "C"` functions not overload the same name?
choices: Because C++ forbids overloading of free functions in general
Because extern "C" functions must be declared in a namespace
Because C linkage forces every parameter to be a pointer
Because C linkage suppresses mangling, so both would need the same flat symbol
mcq.explain: Overload resolution is a compile-time feature that survives to the linker only because mangling encodes parameter types into the symbol name. C linkage removes that encoding, so two overloads would claim one flat symbol; the compiler rejects the second declaration. Putting them in different namespaces does not help either, because the exported C symbol does not encode the namespace.

mcq.prompt: A header declares `extern "C" double mid_c(double, double);` but mid_c.cpp defines the function without including that header. What is the symptom?
choices: The definition silently gets C linkage anyway, and everything works
A compile error in mid_c.cpp
The linker reports an undefined reference to the unmangled name mid_c
The program links and calls the wrong function
mcq.explain: Language linkage is part of a declaration, so a definition compiled without seeing the extern "C" declaration gets an ordinary mangled C++ name. Callers that did see the header emit a reference to the flat name, and nothing defines it. Each translation unit compiles happily on its own — nm on the two objects makes the mismatch obvious, and including the header in the defining file is the fix.

mcq.prompt: `nm main.o` shows `U _Z10spread_bpsRK5Order`. What does that tell you?
choices: main.o references spread_bps but does not define it; some other object must supply it
spread_bps was inlined and no longer exists
spread_bps has internal linkage in main.o
main.o defines spread_bps with a weak binding
mcq.explain: U marks an undefined symbol — a reference the linker must resolve against a definition elsewhere, carried alongside a relocation at the call site. T would be a global definition in .text and W a weak one, typically an emitted inline function; t is the lowercase local form an anonymous-namespace function produces. An `undefined reference` error is simply a U that survived the link.

mcq.prompt: In pricing.o, where does `int tick_count = 0;` normally live on a common ELF toolchain?
choices: .rodata
.bss, with only its size recorded and no zero bytes stored
.data, with eight zero bytes stored in the object
.text
mcq.explain: A zero-initialised global goes to .bss, whose contribution to the file is a size, not bytes — the loader supplies the zeros. A nonzero initialiser would normally move it to .data, where the bytes really are stored. These are common ELF conventions rather than C++ requirements, and an optimiser may fold, relocate or delete the object entirely.

mcq.prompt: `g++ -L. -lpricing main.o -o pricer` fails with an undefined reference, while `g++ main.o -L. -lpricing -o pricer` succeeds. Why?
choices: The archive index is only built when the archive is listed last
Static archives must always precede object files
The linker scans inputs left to right and extracts an archive member only for a symbol that is unresolved at that moment
-L must come after all object files
mcq.explain: Named object files are always included; archive members are demand-loaded. When libpricing.a is scanned first, nothing is unresolved yet, so pricing.o is never extracted — and main.o introduces the reference too late. Put an archive after the objects that need it, and use repetition or --start-group/--end-group for circular archive dependencies.

mcq.prompt: What does a call into an ELF shared library normally cost that a call into a statically linked object does not?
choices: A copy of the arguments through the dynamic loader
Nothing; the two are identical after relocation
A system call per invocation
PLT/GOT indirection, plus loss of inlining because the symbol can be interposed
mcq.explain: After resolution the call goes indirectly through a GOT entry, and lazy binding puts the loader itself on the first call. The subtler cost is that an exported, interposable symbol constrains the optimiser: it cannot inline or bind directly to something LD_PRELOAD might replace. That is why -fvisibility=hidden buys speed as well as a smaller symbol table.

mcq.prompt: Does linking statically give the optimiser a cross-translation-unit view?
choices: No, not by itself — ordinary .o files have already lost the information, so both compilation and the final link must enable LTO
Yes, but only for functions declared inline
No, and LTO cannot help either, because the linker only sees machine code
Yes; that is the main reason to link statically
mcq.explain: An ordinary object file holds machine code from which most source-level information is gone; the linker merging those files does not recover it. Cross-file optimisation needs -flto at compile time so the objects carry intermediate representation, and at link time so the linker plugin hands that IR back to the optimiser. Static linking makes LTO possible over the whole program; it does not perform it.

mcq.prompt: Why must a PImpl class define its destructor in the .cpp file rather than letting the compiler generate it in the header?
choices: Because the destructor must be virtual for the idiom to work
Because unique_ptr's destructor requires a complete Impl, which the header deliberately does not have
Because the header would otherwise need to include <memory>
Because an implicitly declared destructor is not noexcept
mcq.explain: Destroying a std::unique_ptr<Impl> needs Impl to be complete so the deleter can call its destructor. In the header Impl is only declared, so the destructor — and for the same reason the move operations — must be defined in the source file where the class is complete. Writing `= default` there is enough; what matters is where the definition lives, not what it contains.

mcq.prompt: For which kind of class is PImpl the wrong choice?
choices: A class whose private members change frequently
A class whose header currently drags in <string> and <vector>
A coarse service object at a shared-library boundary
A compact Price or Order value type used in an inner loop
mcq.explain: PImpl buys build isolation and ABI stability with a pointer chase and, usually, an allocation per object — a bad trade for a small value type that wants inline storage, trivial movement and compiler-visible members. The other three are exactly the cases it is for. Hide representation deliberately at binary boundaries, and keep hot-path value types transparent to the optimiser.

mcq.prompt: How do linkage and visibility differ?
choices: Visibility applies to functions, linkage to variables
They are two names for the same property
Linkage decides whether declarations in different translation units denote one entity; visibility decides whether the symbol appears in a shared library's dynamic symbol table
Linkage is an ELF concept; visibility is a C++ standard concept
mcq.explain: Linkage is a C++ language property resolved at translation and static link time. Visibility is a shared-object export property: a function can keep external linkage and still be hidden from the dynamic symbol table with -fvisibility=hidden. Hidden symbols also cannot be interposed, which is why the flag helps the optimiser — and why it breaks a dlopen consumer expecting an unexported name.

mcq.prompt: `nm` shows `W mid(double, double)` in both pricing.o and main.o and the program links cleanly. What has happened?
choices: Both are weak/COMDAT definitions of the header-defined inline function; the linker retains one compatible copy and discards the duplicate
The two definitions have internal linkage and are separate entities in the final program
One of them was actually inlined away and the W is a leftover
The linker merged the two bodies into one combined function
mcq.explain: mid is defined in pricing.hpp, so every translation unit that includes the header can emit it — as a weak or COMDAT symbol rather than a strong one. The linker keeps one and drops the rest, which is how common toolchains implement the ODR's inline allowance. It compares names and binding strength, never token sequences, which is exactly why genuinely different weak definitions also link cleanly and leave you with undefined behaviour.

reading.explain: Every parameter is parenthesised, and the macro is still wrong. The expansion is `((3) + (5) % 4)`, and `%` binds tighter than `+`, so the remainder is taken of the step alone: 5 % 4 is 1, plus 3 is 4. The author meant `(3 + 5) % 4`, which is 0. The fix the chapter names is to parenthesise the *complete expansion* as well as each parameter — but the real repair is `constexpr int wrapped(int column, int step) { return (column + step) % columns; }`, where the compiler parses an expression instead of the preprocessor pasting tokens. Answering 0 is assuming the macro means what its name says.

`next_handle` is a template, so `next_handle<Sensor>` and `next_handle<Actuator>` are two different functions, each with its own `issued` object. Both report 1. `next_message` is one ordinary function with one static, so its two calls report 1 and 2. The static's three properties are unchanged in every case — static storage duration, block scope, no linkage — but 'no linkage' is about names, and instantiation is what decides how many objects there are. Expecting '1 2 1 2' treats the template as a single function with a shared counter; per-type counters are exactly what this idiom is used for.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: Both headers chose the guard macro `UTIL_H`. The first one defines it, so when the second is pasted its `#ifndef UTIL_H` is already false and every line between the guards disappears. `Vec2` exists; `Span` was never declared, and `Span label{...}` is an error for an unknown type. The tempting reading is that the guards protect the two headers from each other — they only ever protect one header from being pasted twice, and they identify that header by a macro name the preprocessor matches textually, with no notion of which file it came from. Guard names must be project-unique (`GEOMETRY_UTIL_HPP`), or use `#pragma once`, which identifies the file rather than a name.

Two different initialisations are happening. `base_rate = 48'000` is constant initialisation: it is settled before any dynamic initialisation runs at all, which is why `probe_rate` sees the full 48000 and prints 48 rather than 0. `window = sample_window()` is dynamic, and within one translation unit dynamic initialisation runs in definition order — so at the moment `effective_rate` is initialised, `window` is still the zero it was zero-initialised to. `48000 / 1000 * (0 + 1)` is 48, not the 384 the code reads as. This is the static-initialisation-order fiasco with the ordering *specified*; across translation units the order is unspecified and the same hazard has no fixed answer. Constant-initialise what you can (`constinit` makes the requirement explicit) and reach the rest through construct-on-first-use.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The header declares `class Impl;` and never defines it, which is the whole point of PImpl — but `~Mixer() = default;` written *in the header* asks the compiler to generate the destructor right there, and destroying a `std::unique_ptr<Impl>` instantiates `delete impl_`, which requires a complete `Impl`. libc++ reports it as `invalid application of 'sizeof' to an incomplete type`. The fix is not to abandon the default: declare `~Mixer();` in the header and write `Mixer::~Mixer() = default;` in the source file, where `Impl` is complete. The same applies to the move operations. Reading this as 'unique_ptr can hold an incomplete type' is half right — it can hold one; it just cannot be *destroyed* against one.

`normalise` has one body, and its unqualified call to `in_metres` resolves separately for each instantiation: argument-dependent lookup finds `si::in_metres` for a `Metre` and `imperial::in_metres` for a `Foot`, so 2.0 metres stays 2 and 10 feet become 3.048. That is the mechanism behind the ODR's strictness about name lookup: 'matching token sequences' is necessary but not sufficient, because the identical tokens `in_metres(length)` can denote different entities in different contexts. Two headers with byte-identical inline bodies can therefore still violate the ODR — and unlike a duplicate symbol, nothing diagnoses it.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The opaque-handle boundary is built correctly — incomplete struct in the API, C linkage, the creating side owning destruction — and it still cannot save the caller from itself. `registry_add` returns the new plugin count, the `if` sees 2 and destroys the registry, and the next line calls through the freed handle. AddressSanitizer reports heap-use-after-free at `handle->plugins`. The reading to resist is that the handle is 'just an integer-like token' the library can validate: it is a pointer to freed storage, the library has no way to know, and a C API's return codes cannot express a mistake the caller made after destruction. This is the ownership cost of an opaque handle — it buys a narrow ABI and gives up every lifetime guarantee C++ would have provided.

`at_namespace_scope` is a namespace-scope object with a dynamic initialiser, so its initialisation runs before `main` — 'N' is appended first. (`trace` is defined earlier in the same translation unit, so it is constructed first and is ready to be appended to.) `main` then appends 'M'. The local `static` inside `cached_limit` is not initialised until control first passes through its declaration, which is the first call, and the once-only guard means the second call skips the initialiser entirely — one 'L', and it lands after 'M'. Expecting 'NLM' assumes the local static is initialised alongside the namespace-scope one; that lazy initialisation is precisely what makes construct-on-first-use a fix for the ordering hazard, and it is also the guard check the Latency Lens mentions on every call until initialisation completes.

writing.prompt: A tilemap header currently contains `int loaded_tiles = 0;`, a full definition of `tile_index`, and a declaration of `tile_count` that nothing defines. Two .cpp files include it. Rewrite the header/source pair so both link errors disappear, and annotate each entity with how many definitions the program may contain and which build stage would have complained.
checklist: The header has an include guard with a project-unique macro name
The mutable global is extern in the header and defined exactly once in the source half
The small hot function stays in the header but is marked inline; the non-inline function is only declared there
A definition for the previously undefined function is supplied in the source half
Comments distinguish the multiple-definition failure from the undefined-reference failure, and note that neither is a compile error
writing.notes: The asymmetry is worth holding onto: a compile error belongs to one translation unit, while both of these belong to the relationship between translation units, so neither can appear until the linker has every object in view. `inline` is what buys the right to keep `tile_index` in the header — it means 'identical definitions may appear in several translation units', not 'substitute the body at the call site', and the toolchain implements it by emitting a weak/COMDAT symbol and keeping one.

writing.prompt: Retire two macros from a tilemap: `#define WRAPPED(c, s) ((c) + (s) % COLUMNS)`, whose parameters are all parenthesised and which still computes the wrong thing, and `#define PICK_LARGER(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))`. The replacements must satisfy two properties: `wrapped(3, step)` must group the addition before the remainder, and an argument with a side effect must be evaluated exactly once. Assert both properties in the code, and keep the one macro that has no language-level replacement.
checklist: wrapped is a constexpr function whose grouping is the author's, not the preprocessor's
The larger-of is a function template (or a constrained function) taking each argument once
A comment names the specific defect in each macro: unparenthesised expansion, and repeated substitution of the argument tokens
A static_assert or equivalent checks that a side-effecting argument is evaluated exactly once
An #ifdef NDEBUG block defines an inline constexpr bool, and a comment says why this use of the preprocessor stays
writing.notes: Parenthesising the parameters fixes only half of the precedence problem — the expansion itself sits inside a larger expression and needs its own parentheses too. Repeated evaluation has no parenthesis-level fix at all: a macro substitutes tokens and has no parameter objects, so `PICK_LARGER(next(), 0)` calls `next` twice by construction. Note also that the replacements gain something macros never had: names that obey scope and namespaces, so they cannot rewrite an unrelated identifier three headers later.

writing.prompt: Publish a units header containing six things: a class, a compile-time constant usable as a template argument in every translation unit, a class constant whose address is taken, an inline conversion function, a function whose single definition lives elsewhere, and a mutable global whose single definition lives elsewhere. Annotate each with declaration/definition and with how many the program may contain, then supply the source half.
checklist: The compile-time constant is an inline constexpr variable, with a comment saying what inline buys
The class constant is a static constexpr member, with a note that C++17 made it implicitly inline so taking its address needs no out-of-class definition
The function and the mutable global appear as declarations only, and both are defined once in the source half
A comment on the inline function explains that matching token sequences is stricter than equivalent results
Each entity's comment states declaration, definition, or both, and the permitted count
writing.notes: The two failure modes sit on either side of this header. Define the global in the header and every including translation unit emits a strong symbol with that name — `multiple definition`. Define it nowhere and the compiler is satisfied by the declaration in each translation unit — `undefined reference`. The dangerous middle case is the class: repeated definitions are legal only when they are the *same* definition, and a member added in one header and not another produces matching mangled names, a clean link, and two files disagreeing about the layout.

writing.prompt: Write one translation unit containing three counters that differ in all three properties: one that lives for the program but that no other translation unit can denote by name, one that any translation unit may denote, and one per instantiated type. Annotate each with its storage duration, its scope and its linkage, and say which of the three does not apply to the functions themselves.
checklist: The translation-unit-private state is in an anonymous namespace, with a note that namespace-scope static could not also localise a type
The shareable counter is an ordinary namespace-scope definition, with a comment giving the extern declaration another translation unit would write
The per-type counter is a function-local static inside a function template
Each comment states all three properties explicitly
A comment notes that functions have no storage duration, because that classification applies to objects and references
writing.notes: The three properties are genuinely independent, and `static` is the keyword that most obscures that: at block scope it sets storage duration, at namespace scope it sets linkage, and inside a class it does neither. Ask which property the context changes. Note too that visibility in the source text implies nothing on its own — the function-local static is unreachable by name from anywhere else and still lives for the whole program, while the namespace-scope object is reachable from every translation unit that declares it.

writing.prompt: Another .cpp in this project already defines a struct named `Node` and a helper named `depth_of` at namespace scope, with different members. Rewrite this file so a collision is impossible, publish exactly one name from it, and explain in comments what the link would have done without the change and why it would not have been diagnosed.
checklist: Both the helper type and the helper function are inside an anonymous namespace
A comment states that namespace-scope static cannot localise a type, which is why the anonymous namespace is the rule
A comment states that two definitions of the same externally linked class commonly link clean and misbehave at run time, with no diagnostic required
Exactly one externally linked entry point remains outside the anonymous namespace
The published signature does not mention the internal-linkage type
writing.notes: The silent failure is the reason for the rule. Out-of-class inline member definitions become weak or COMDAT symbols with the same mangled name, so the linker keeps one and discards the rest without comparing bodies — and the file whose layout lost then reads and writes members its own objects do not have. Note the last checklist item too: an internal-linkage type in an externally linked function's signature is a design error, because no other translation unit can name the type it would have to pass.

writing.prompt: Expose an audio sampler to a C consumer that wants to be called back when frames arrive. Write the shared header and the implementation: an opaque handle, a callback registration taking a plain function pointer plus user state, a push function, and destruction. The API must be parsable as C, must report errors without exceptions, and must not depend on overloading.
checklist: The handle is an incomplete struct type in the API, never the C++ class
Every exported declaration is inside an extern "C" block guarded by #ifdef __cplusplus
The callback is a C function pointer with an accompanying void* for user state, not a std::function or a capturing lambda
Failures are reported as return codes, and no exception escapes an extern "C" function
The creating side supplies destruction, and a comment notes that C-linkage names cannot be overloaded
writing.notes: The `void* user_data` parameter is doing the work a lambda capture would do in C++, and it is not optional: a C function pointer carries no state, so without it the consumer has nowhere to put its own context. Note also the mangling trap the chapter names — if the definitions were compiled without seeing these `extern "C"` declarations they would acquire mangled C++ names and the link would fail on the unmangled ones, which is why the source file includes the same header rather than trusting the signatures to line up.

writing.prompt: Convert a tokenizer whose header exposes a std::string and a std::vector<std::string> into a PImpl class. The contract: the header must not include <string> or <vector>, the public class must be exactly one pointer wide and stay that width when a member is added to the implementation, and the type must be movable. Get the special member functions in the right half of the file and say why.
checklist: The header declares a nested Impl class without defining it and holds a std::unique_ptr<Impl>
The destructor is declared in the header and defined in the source half where Impl is complete
Move operations are declared in the header and defaulted in the source half; copy is deleted or written deliberately
The header includes neither <string> nor <vector>
A static_assert (or equivalent) checks that the public class is one pointer wide
writing.notes: Writing `~Tokenizer() = default;` in the header is the mistake this exercise is built around: it asks the compiler to generate the destructor where `Impl` is still incomplete, and destroying a `unique_ptr<Impl>` instantiates `delete` on it. The same applies to the move operations, which is why they are declared in one half and defaulted in the other. What you buy is a private member change that recompiles one file instead of every user, and a `sizeof` that does not move — the ABI-stability half of the deal. What you pay is a pointer chase and an allocation per object, so keep this off per-event value types.

writing.prompt: A shared library should export exactly one factory function, one global, and one polymorphic interface type — nothing else. Write the export-macro header fragment for a build using -fvisibility=hidden, apply it to all three, and include the build flags and the command that proves the resulting export surface. Note in a comment what breaks if this is applied too aggressively.
checklist: The macro expands to __attribute__((visibility("default"))) when building the library and to nothing otherwise
The build-side branch is selected by a macro defined only during the library's own build
The macro is applied to a function declaration, an extern variable declaration and a class
A comment gives the -fvisibility=hidden build flags and an nm -D command that inspects the actual export surface
A comment states that a polymorphic type crossing the boundary needs its type information exported, and that hiding a symbol a dlopen consumer expects is a breaking change
writing.notes: Visibility is not linkage. These entities keep external linkage and link normally inside the library; visibility only decides whether they appear in the dynamic symbol table the loader searches. The class case is the one that catches people: the vtable and type information are separate symbols, and a consumer that catches an exception by reference or performs a dynamic_cast is comparing type_info across the boundary, so hiding the type breaks something the call itself would never have revealed. Treat the macro as part of the library's ABI contract.
